title: Knowing what you know
hook: to know what you know and know what you don't: that is knowledge (Analects 2.17)
tomorrow: who should you copy, and what do you do with a bad example?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yan Hui, the student whose learning showed in his temper: learn and practice. Today, a different student, and a different weakness: the one who answered first, and checked later.
screen: `LEARN AND PRACTICE.` → `THE ONE WHO ANSWERED FIRST.`

segments.voice: In a meeting someone drops an acronym, and the whole table nods. Nobody wants to be the one who asks what it stands for. The Analects has a puzzle about exactly that. Confucius turns to one student, Zilu, whose personal name is Yu, and offers to teach him what knowledge is. Then he gives a definition that's half about not knowing. Why would knowledge need not-knowing inside it? And why say it to Zilu, of all people?
screen: `THE WHOLE TABLE NODS.` → `YU, SHALL I TEACH YOU?` → `HALF OF IT IS NOT KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in James Legge's translation: "When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;—this is knowledge." Now meet Zilu in another passage. Confucius says that if he governed, his first task would be to set names right, so that words match things. Zilu shoots back: you're wide of the mark! Confucius answers him bluntly: how unpolished you are, Yu. A gentleman holds back about what he doesn't know. So the puzzle solves itself, on one reading: the definition was cut to fit the student. Elsewhere Confucius says Zilu loves daring even more than he does. Brave, quick people fill gaps with confidence, and it often works, until it doesn't. Confucius doesn't tell him to know more. He tells him to see where his knowing stops. The teaching, plainly: in the Confucian tradition, the junzi, the exemplary person, is honest about the edge of their knowledge, because when words don't match things, actions go wrong too. One for tonight: Confucius's definition of knowledge has two halves, and the second half is saying I don't know. In the Analects that sentence isn't a hole in your knowledge. It's part of it.
screen: `HOLD WHAT YOU KNOW. ALLOW WHAT YOU DON'T.` · `YOU'RE WIDE OF THE MARK!` · `CUT TO FIT THE STUDENT.` · `THE JUNZI KNOWS WHERE HIS KNOWING STOPS.` · then, large: `THAT IS KNOWLEDGE.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been nodding along to: a word, a fact, something at work or at home. For these two minutes, say it quietly to yourself: I don't know this yet. Then picture the one person you could ask, and the exact question.
Knowing what you know: Confucius's knowledge in two halves, the part you hold and the edge you admit.
Keep this one: that is knowledge, and knowing where your knowing stops counts too. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of the Analects take 2.17 as a check on honesty in learning; in the Confucian tradition, admitting the limits of what you know belongs to the exemplary person, the junzi.

fork.setup: a new coworker asks how a system works that you only half understand. what's the Analects answer?
options: explain the half you know, and say plainly where your knowing stops.
explain all of it confidently; doubt makes you look unready.
say you know nothing about it, so you can't be wrong.
fork.reveal: 2.17: hold what you know, allow what you don't. the two halves together are knowledge; hiding the half you know isn't it either.

original.note: Chinese zhi, to know, knowledge: the word Confucius repeats through Analects 2.17.

trapdoor: what you thought: knowledge means having the answers.
what it means: Confucius defines it in two halves: holding what you know, and allowing what you don't.
what a scholar hears: 2.17 is addressed to Zilu by his name Yu; 13.3 shows the same student answering before he knows, on setting names right.

knowing enough to answer any question asked

chat.says: a patient asked if a shot's covered. i said 'probably yes' to sound sure. was that bad?
options: Confucius would say: 'i don't know, let me check.' Admitting that is half of knowledge.
It's fine. Confucius says sounding sure is what makes people trust you.
Next time say you can't help at all. That's the safest kind of honest.
chat.meaning: In Analects 2.17, knowledge means holding what you know and allowing what you don't. Guessing to sound sure breaks the second half.

tie.story: Zilu answered before he knew, and Confucius told him knowledge includes allowing what you don't know.
tie.friend: Zoe can tell the patient she'll check the coverage, instead of guessing to sound sure.
tie.you: where are you nodding along to something you don't know?
